chapters.title: 1. How My Passion Became My Profession
chapters.summary: Rupal Bhansali opens with her Bombay childhood where her aunt teaches her to love geometry and her father trades small lots of shares at the kitchen table, illustrated by a brokerage contract note from Dalal Street, grounding passion in household arithmetic. The anecdote of her arriving in the US for graduate study with two suitcases and a scholarship, then interning at a fund where she is told to follow the model, and replying that the model is the problem, shows contrarian roots early. A figure maps her career path from Sorrell to Oppenheimer as a learning curve where each role expanded her circle from India to global emerging markets, illustrated as a passport stamp collage. The chapter recounts her time at MacKay Shields covering emerging equities where she questions why a database of historical averages should dictate future, shown as a database versus search engine contrast table. The concept is that passion becomes profession when curiosity about being right when everyone else is wrong becomes a daily hunt, not a slogan. She shares the story of being told emerging markets are un-investable at the moment she finds them cheapest, a fund flow chart showing outflows at the trough. The closing reflection is that non-consensus is not contrarian for its own sake but empathetic curiosity about what the consensus assumes, illustrated as an assumptions audit sheet she still uses before any pitch. The episode matters because it shows how preparation, incentives, and willingness to endure uncertainty compound into an edge that looks like luck in hindsight but was deliberately engineered. chapters.title: 2. 'And' Not 'Or'
chapters.summary: Bhansali argues great allocation is both, not either, opening with the anecdote of an institutional board that forced a choice between growth or value, developed or emerging, and she draws an and bridge on a whiteboard, illustrated as a Venn where both sides overlap in real companies. A case study of a consumer company that is both defensive and growing, illustrated as a quadrant where low beta meets high reinvestment, shows and thinking. A figure maps horizons: short-term traders see or, long-term owners see and, a time horizon chart where volatility smooths and fundamentals dominate. She recounts a debate where a colleague says stocks or bonds, and she shows a holding that behaves like a bond in downside and a stock in upside, illustrated as a payoff diagram that is convex. The chapter tells the story of her balanced emerging fund that owned both growth compounds and distressed cyclicals, a holdings map where geographies and styles mix. The concept is that and thinking requires rejecting false trade-offs imposed by benchmarks and peer boxes. A final illustration shows a both-and checklist where any pitch must answer how it contributes to both resilience and upside, a discipline that prevents style drift while remaining flexible. The lesson is that the world is not binary, so portfolios need not be. chapters.title: 3. Stocks or Bonds?
chapters.summary: The question is literal and portfolios should be agnostic. Bhansali opens with the anecdote of a client who insists on a strategic 60-40 and she asks what if both are expensive, illustrated by a valuation scatter where equity yield and bond yield both sit at historic lows. A case study of an emerging market sovereign that she bought as a bond when yields were high, then sold to buy its equity when currency devaluation made equities cheap, shown as a rotation arrow diagram stock-bond-stock, demonstrates opportunism. A figure maps real yield versus nominal illusion, where high nominal with high inflation is actually low real, the adjustment she applies via a real yield chart. She recounts the 1990s Asian crisis where she bought Korean debt when spreads were distressed, illustrated by a spread spike chart. The concept is opportunistic asset allocation across the capital structure based on where compensation is, not where mandate says to be, illustrated as a capital stack where value migrates between senior debt and equity as conditions change. A checklist for stocks-or-bonds decisions compares implied return versus risk for each, forcing a side-by-side that peers avoid because it crosses silos. The chapter ends with a reminder that the same company can be a buy as debt and a sell as equity at different prices, proving labels obscure value. chapters.title: 4. To Stand Apart, You Must Stand Alone
chapters.summary: Standing apart requires standing alone socially. Bhansali tells of her downgrade of a beloved emerging market consumer darling while the street upgraded, illustrated by a recommendation dispersion chart where she sits alone. The anecdote of a morning meeting where she is told everyone disagrees and she replies that is the point, shows temperament. A figure maps her information diet: no trading floor, few conferences, primary documents and field visits, illustrated as an inverted funnel where consensus noise is filtered. She recounts a field trip to a Brazilian retailer where she counts trucks at distribution centers, a photograph of a dusty yard with logged counts, contradicting management guidance. The chapter details the loneliness cost, where tracking error spikes before payoff, illustrated as a tracking error versus excess return time series where pain precedes gain. The concept is that non-consensus without process is just contrarianism, so she pairs independence with a checklist that validates solitude with data. A final illustration shows a solitude infrastructure: calendar blocks for reading, a rule to not check prices intraday, a peer group of one trusted devil's advocate, a system that makes standing alone sustainable rather than heroic. The lesson: if you cannot tolerate being alone, you cannot be non-consensus. chapters.title: 5. Score Upset Victories
chapters.summary: Bhansali reframes investing as a sports tournament where favorites often lose, but upsets pay disproportionately. She opens with the 2015 Rugby World Cup where Japan beats South Africa, illustrated by a bracket where the upset flips the pool, analogous to an emerging small-cap beating a guru stock. A case study details her investment in a Korean bank consensus deemed un-investable due to governance fears, illustrated by a governance discount chart that priced in nationalization even as capital ratios improved, a governance versus price scatter that will later gap close. Another anecdote tells of buying a Russian retailer when sanctions made it untouchable, illustrated by a sanctions timeline where price bottoms at sanction headlines, then recovers. A figure maps base rates: favorites win often but pay little, upsets win rarely but pay heavily, a payoff matrix where the expected value favors patient upset hunting when odds are mispriced. She introduces the concept of scoring upset victories by buying option-like equities where downside is capped but upside is open, illustrated as a payoff diagram. A final illustration shows a tournament bracket for a portfolio where each holding is an upset bet with uncorrelated drivers, so portfolio variance is dampened while upside is convex. The chapter ends with the discipline of sizing upsets smaller but owning many, a sizing rule that respects low hit rate but high payoff. chapters.title: 6. Do No Harm
chapters.summary: Do no harm is her Hippocratic investing principle. Bhansali opens with the anecdote of a manager who avoided a crowded Turkish bank not because he knew it would fall but because he knew he could not know its loan book, illustrated by an opacity diagram where disclosure gaps hide risk. A figure contrasts upside of commission versus downside of client harm, the same Hippocratic asymmetry, with a harm versus gain bar where harm dominates. She recounts her rule to avoid leveraged, opaque financials in fragile regimes, illustrated as a risk map where leverage and opacity intersect as a no-go zone. The chapter tells the story of passing on a hyped Chinese property developer, later revealed to be insolvent, illustrated by a leverage tower graphic. The concept is first, avoid permanent loss, not first, maximize gain, illustrated as a drawdown chart where a 50 percent loss needs 100 percent to recover. An illustration shows her health checklist for any holding: can you explain leverage, currency, and governance simply, yes or no gates. The closing lesson is that non-consensus does not mean owning everything contrarian, it means having a hard no list that keeps you in the game. chapters.title: 7. False Positives and Negatives
chapters.summary: Signal errors are inevitable, so design to minimize the costlier kind. Bhansali tells of her false positive where she bought a Brazilian utility that screened cheap but regulators capped tariffs, illustrated as a value trap where reported yield hides regulatory ceiling, a price versus allowed return chart. Another anecdote recounts a false negative where she avoided an Indian IT services firm as expensive while its ROIC compounded quietly, shown as a compounding chart that outruns its multiple. A decision matrix figure reproduces the medical test analogy: false positive, you own a bad cheap stock, false negative, you miss a compounder, costs differ. The chapter introduces her error cost weighting, where false positives that lose capital weigh heavier than false negatives that forgo gain, illustrated as weighted error bars. She shares her practice of writing a kill thesis before buying, listing what would prove the thesis false, illustrated as a kill thesis template. An illustration shows base rates for each error by sector, where in emerging cyclicals false positives dominate, so she demands higher hurdle. The concept is Bayesian updating: update slowly when evidence is noisy, quickly when kill thesis triggers, a updating speed diagram. The closing reflection is that humility about error type shapes sizing and diversification more than any return forecast. chapters.title: 8. Ditch the Database, Embrace the Search Engine
chapters.summary: The titular chapter argues that backward-looking screens create consensus by construction. Bhansali opens with the anecdote of a quant screen that ranked a Korean auto supplier as low quality because historical ROE was low, while she visits the factory and sees automation that will double returns, illustrated by a factory floor photograph with robots. A figure contrasts database attributes, standardized, lagged, comparable, with search engine attributes, forward-looking, mosaic, context-rich, a contrast table. She tells the story of a management meeting where the CEO explains a new distribution network not yet in the database, illustrated as a network diagram that will show up in results only after the price has moved. A chart shows factor backtests beating while forward returns fade, the database decay curve. The concept is mosaic research: assemble non-database fragments, channel checks, patents, hiring patterns, into a forward view, illustrated as mosaic tiles forming a picture before the database quantifies it. An illustration shows her search engine workflow: question, hypotheses, kill questions, field checks, variant view, repeated as a loop. The chapter closes with a warning that embracing the search engine requires tolerating ambiguity longer than the database crowd, illustrating patience as the price of variant insight. chapters.title: 9. From Victim to Victor
chapters.summary: Lessons from losers turn victims into victors. Bhansali recounts a 2008 loss in a Russian bank where she was early and wrong, illustrated as a drawdown diary where she notes the lesson never argue with a government that can change the rules. The anecdote of keeping a mistake journal, illustrated by a page with columns what I believed, what happened, what I will change, shows systematic learning. Another story tells of a distressed sovereign where she was victim to currency devaluation, later victor by hedging differently, illustrated as a currency hedge payoff comparison. A figure maps victim versus victor mindset, where the victim blames market and the victor extracts a rule, illustrated as a branching tree. She shares her rule after the Russian loss: avoid state-controlled entities where minority rights are optional, illustrated as a governance risk matrix. The concept is that non-consensus inevitably produces losers, but losers that teach a transferable rule raise the hit rate next time. An illustration shows her post-mortem cadence, quarterly review where every closed position gets a victim-victor tag. The closing lesson is that resilience in emerging markets is built from a catalogue of scars that become filters, not from a record of wins. chapters.title: 10. Value Investing = Margin of Safety
chapters.summary: Value is not low multiple, it is margin of safety calibrated to what you can know about a business in an emerging regime. Bhansali opens with the anecdote of buying an Indonesian consumer company at what looked like high multiple but with a distribution moat that made earnings highly predictable, illustrated as a moat diagram where distribution density creates predictability. A figure decomposes margin of safety into balance sheet, business stability, and price, a three-part bar where each can compensate for the others. She tells the story of avoiding a cheap Brazilian steel mill where balance sheet was levered and business cyclical, illustrated as a fragile bar where none of the three gives safety. A chart shows her normalized earnings versus reported, where she adjusts for commodity peaks before capitalizing, the mirror of Marks's profit cycle caution. The chapter recounts a meeting with a founder who explains his family's fifty-year view, illustrated as a family tree, giving confidence in business stability that a database cannot. The concept is that margin of safety in emerging markets must overweight business and balance sheet because price alone cannot compensate for opacity. An illustration shows her safety checklist with kill questions for each pillar, applied uniformly so cheapness never alone justifies. The lesson: value is safety, not statistically cheap. chapters.title: 11. Sizzle Fizzles, Patience Prospers
chapters.summary: Sizzle versus substance is the temptation of story stocks. Bhansali recounts a hot new emerging tech IPO with sizzle, illustrated by a prospectus cover with hockey stick forecasts, that she passes while the crowd chases. A figure maps sizzle as media mentions versus substance as free cash conversion, where the two diverge. The anecdote of buying a boring Indian bearings maker with no sizzle but steady ROIC, illustrated as a factory photo and a flat but rising cash flow chart, shows patience rewarded. Another illustration shows the patience edge as a time arbitrage chart where short-horizon holders sell on noise, long-horizon owners collect compounding. She tells the story of a sizzle stock that triples then collapses, while her boring compounder doubles steadily, illustrated as two price paths diverging after hype fades. The concept is that patience prospers because most participants cannot wait, creating a structural premium for holding quiet compounders. The closing reflection is that emerging markets are especially sizzle prone, so patience is a moat. chapters.title: 12. North Star
chapters.summary: The north star is a principles compass that keeps non-consensus from drifting into contrarianism for its own sake. Bhansali closes with the anecdote of writing her north star on a card: protect capital, respect risk, be curious, illustrated by the card facsimile. A figure maps her north star as a constellation where each principle is a star, and any position must be visible from all stars to be taken. She recounts turning down a lucrative mandate that would have forced style drift, illustrated as a mandate drift diagram where asset gathering pulls away from principle. Another story tells of mentoring a young analyst who wants to chase sizzle, and she hands him the north star card and asks which star the trade serves. The chapter ties back to the opening Bombay kitchen table, now with her own children watching her read, illustrated by a home photograph, completing the circle. The concept is that a north star makes saying no easier than saying yes, so the portfolio remains coherent across regimes. An illustration shows annual north star review, where each holding is scored against the constellation. The book ends with a special message from me to you, a one-page letter reproduced urging readers to define their own north star before hunting for upset victories, because process without purpose is just activity.
